title: Root cause caution — spoken follow-up
situation: In a technical discussion, latency rose after a release. You must answer aloud accurately without overstating the evidence.
instructions: Say aloud why latency rising after a release does not by itself identify the release as the cause.

vocabulary.meaning: wording that separates what was observed from what is inferred, so that a hypothesis is not reported as a finding
an observation whose outcome differs depending on which hypothesis is true, and which is therefore worth performing

expectedElements: Observation and hypothesis are worded differently
At least one competing explanation is raised
A check that would discriminate is proposed
modelAnswer: Latency rose after the release, and I want to keep those two facts in the order I just said them. What we observed is a correlation in time. The release is a candidate, and it is a good one, but so is the traffic increase that started the same morning, and so is the database maintenance window. If I report the release as the cause now and I am wrong, we roll back for nothing and lose the real cause. The evidence that separates them is cheap to obtain: compare latency on the instances that did not receive the release yet. If they slowed too, it is not the release. I can have that in ten minutes.
commonMistakes: Reporting a hypothesis in the wording reserved for a finding
Proposing a rollback before any observation distinguishes the candidates
variants: Answer again when a manager asks you to roll back immediately.
